issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette: Harold had always taken pride in his independence. As a database administrator, he spent most of his days working from home, surrounded by screens and wires that hummed with a comforting familiarity. But all of this changed two years ago when Harold was diagnosed with stage III cancer. The treatment was grueling – surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy left him weak and exhausted. There were times when Harold thought he wouldn't make it, when the pain and nausea felt like they would consume him whole. One particular moment during his hospital stay still haunted Harold. He had been wheeled into a crowded elevator to be taken for a treatment session, and as the doors closed, he felt a wave of panic wash over him. The smell of disinfectant and stale air seemed to intensify, making his stomach turn. When the doors finally opened, Harold stumbled out into the bright lights of the hospital corridor, feeling like he was going to pass out. Since then, Harold had been on high alert at home, always scanning his surroundings for potential threats. He would sit in his favorite armchair, eyes darting back and forth between the windows, waiting for...what, exactly? He didn't know, but the sense of being "on guard" was constant. At night, he'd lie awake, feeling like he could hear every creak and groan of the house, convinced that someone – or something – was lurking just out of sight. When memories of his illness crept into Harold's mind, they felt more vivid than any ordinary recollection. He would catch a whiff of disinfectant at the grocery store and suddenly be transported back to that hospital elevator, his heart racing like it did on that terrible day. The smells seemed to unlock a door in his mind, flooding him with images of himself lying helpless in a hospital bed. Harold couldn't shake the feeling that the world was a treacherous place, full of hidden dangers waiting to pounce. His faith, once strong and reassuring, had been shaken by his illness. He felt lost and alone, like he'd been left to fend for himself in a universe devoid of meaning or purpose. Even now, as Harold sat at home, staring blankly at the screens that used to bring him such joy, he couldn't help but feel like his body was betraying him. His heart still racing from some phantom threat, his mind perpetually on edge – it all felt like a cruel joke. Why should he have made it through the cancer only to be left with this constant sense of dread? As the months dragged on, Harold's isolation grew. He stopped taking calls from friends and family, preferring to hole up at home where it was safe. His work suffered as well – how could he focus on database queries when his mind was always scanning for threats? His clients began to complain about missed deadlines and shoddy workmanship, but Harold just couldn't seem to care. It wasn't until he received a stern letter from the company threatening termination that Harold realized things had gone too far. Something needed to change – but what? He felt stuck in this endless loop of fear and hypervigilance, unsure how to break free. That's when Harold finally made up his mind to seek help, hoping against hope that someone could show him a way out of the darkness that had consumed his life.
